item.title: AL, whose activities now banned, holds rally in Shariatpur, 3 detained
item.description:
The Awami League, whose activities are now banned, held a protest march and a motorbike rally on the Dhaka–Shariatpur regional highway in Naria upazila of Shariatpur.

Police conducted a raid during the event, seizing three motorcycles and arresting three people. Later, a case was filed against them under the Anti-Terrorism Act.

The event was held yesterday, Monday, in the Gagri jora area of Naria upazila. A 1-minute-29-second video of the event has circulated on social media.

Leaders and activists of the Awami League, Chhatra League and Jubo League, who are in hiding, shared the video on their Facebook accounts. The activities of the Chhatra League and the Jubo League are also now banned.

A video circulated on Facebook shows more than 100 people walking along the Dhaka–Shariatpur road carrying a banner that reads, “Mourning rally marking 15 August.” They were heard chanting slogans in the names of Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, ousted former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and former Shariatpur-1 MP Iqbal Hossain.

Another video shows Awami League leaders and activists holding a motorbike rally with a large number of motorcycles in the Gagri jora area, on the slope of the Kotapara Bridge along the Dhaka–Shariatpur road.

The rally disrupted traffic on both sides of the road. As the location was close to Palong Model Police Station, police conducted a raid and arrested three people along with three motorcycles.

Police said the arrested men are Tushar Ahmed, 23, Al Amin Sardar, 26, and Riad Munshi, 49, all from Shariatpur Sadar upazila. They were handed over to Naria police last night. Later, on Tuesday morning, a sub-inspector (SI) of Naria police filed a case against them under the Anti-Terrorism Act.

Naria police SI Jasim Uddin told Prothom Alo that some people affiliated with the Awami League held a procession and a motorbike rally on the Dhaka–Shariatpur road. Three people were arrested from the spot and a case was filed against them. Police are trying to identify and arrest others by examining videos of the programme.

item.title: GOT fame Kit Harington joins 'Harry Potter' Season 2 as Gilderoy Lockhart
item.description:
Game of Thrones (GOT) fame Kit Harington is set to join HBO's 'Harry Potter' series in Season 2 as Gilderoy Lockhart, replacing Nicholas Hoult in the role, HBO Max has confirmed on its official social media handle.

The recasting comes after scheduling conflicts made it impossible for Hoult to continue with the production, as per Deadline.

In an Instagram post, HBO Max wrote, "Before we begin year two at Hogwarts, there has been a slight change due to scheduling: Kit Harington will now be stepping into the role of Gilderoy Lockhart."

Why is Harry Potter still so popular in the Muggles world?

Hoult, who was originally cast as Lockhart, had two pre-existing projects that HBO had to work around.

When filming Lockhart's scenes shifted within the Season 2 production schedule, accommodating those commitments was no longer feasible, leading to the Superman actor's departure from the role.

Harington was subsequently approached by HBO. Available to take on the part, the actor also had a connection to the character; he previously voiced Gilderoy Lockhart in 'Harry Potter: The Full-Cast Audio Editions', which were released late last year.

In a featurette released by Audible around the audio editions, Harington spoke about his long-standing affection for JK Rowling's Harry Potter books. The actor recalled that he was the same age as Harry when the first novel was published.

"I read it, and like so many generations, I was entranced, and then I was a huge fan all through my teenage years," he said.

Lockhart is a major character in Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets, the second book in Rowling's series.

The character was played by Kenneth Branagh in the second Harry Potter film. A vain, boastful and fame-obsessed wizard, Lockhart is known for his expertise in Memory Charms and is recruited by Albus Dumbledore as Hogwarts' Defence Against the Dark Arts professor.

Season 2 of Harry Potter was greenlit in May and is scheduled to begin filming this fall. The production is moving ahead before the Christmas premiere of Season 1, titled Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone.

The series will air on HBO and stream exclusively on HBO Max.

Dominic McLaughlin stars as Harry Potter, with Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley and Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger.

Returning cast members include Nick Frost as Rubeus Hagrid, John Lithgow as Albus Dumbledore, Paapa Essiedu as Severus Snape and Janet McTeer as Professor McGonagall.

The series is written and executive produced by showrunner Francesca Gardiner, with Mark Mylod serving as executive producer and directing multiple episodes.

Jon Brown, who wrote for Season 1, has been elevated to co-showrunner for Season 2 alongside Gardiner.

For Harington, the role marks his third series for HBO. He previously played Jon Snow across all eight seasons of Game of Thrones and currently stars as a series regular on HBO's Industry.

item.title: Murder of Rangpur family: Case handed to DB
item.description:
A murder case filed over the killing of four members of a family in Rangpur has been handed over to the Detective Branch (DB) of Rangpur Metropolitan Police for investigation, amid questions from the victims’ relatives over the police account of the killings.
The family has demanded a wider probe, saying two people could not have carried out the brutal killing of all four members.
Metropolitan DB Deputy Commissioner Sanatan Chakraborty confirmed the case was transferred from Kotwali police station and said it would be investigated seriously.
“We have received the case documents. The case will be investigated by considering it seriously,” he said.
The victims were recently retired Rangpur Zilla School teacher Ganapati Chakraborty, 65, his wife Pritilata Chakraborty, 50, their daughter Prarthi Chakraborty, 24, a master’s student, and their 12-year-old son Priyam Chakraborty, a Class V student at Rangpur Zilla School.
The four were found dead at their home in the city’s Masuapara area late Saturday night, about two days after the killings allegedly took place. Relatives became concerned after repeated calls to the family went unanswered. Fire Service personnel later broke open the locked door and found one body inside a room and three others near the rooftop.
Police subsequently arrested Siddhartha Das, 23, and Mugdha Das, 19, and said they had confessed to the killings.
According to the police, the two suspects were consuming yaba pills on the rooftop when Ganapati confronted them. They allegedly strangled him, his wife and daughter before killing Priyam inside the house. Police also said the suspects tried to make the killings look like a robbery.
The police account, however, has been met with skepticism from relatives, teachers, students and local residents, who have demanded a fresh investigation and questioned whether two suspects could have killed the entire family.
Gopinath Chakraborty, Ganapati’s elder brother and the complainant in the case, said a major force could be behind the killings and those operating behind the scenes must be identified and brought to justice.
“It is not possible in any way for two people to kill four members of a family,” he said.
Speaking at a Shraddha and prayer ceremony at the family’s residence on Tuesday afternoon, Gopinath expressed frustration and anger over the investigation.
“My brother Ganapati was a very good person. I do not think he could have had any enemies,” he said.
“I filed the case hoping to get justice. The police must properly investigate and identify the killers and their godfathers. Otherwise, we will have nothing to do but silently shed tears,” he added.
Ganapati’s niece Trishna Talukdar also called for a proper investigation, saying no innocent person should be punished.
“The killing of my uncle Ganapati, his wife, son and daughter was the work of a gang. Such a brutal killing could not have been carried out by two people,” she said.
“We cannot even slaughter a pigeon; our hands tremble. And two young boys killed four people. We have to believe this?” she said, breaking down in tears.
Rangpur Puja Celebration Council Vice-President and priest Dhiman Chakraborty said he believed a larger group could be involved.
“I have heard that the two people arrested by police have confessed. But it is necessary to find out who else was involved and why the killings took place,” he said.
Relatives of Ganapati, members of the Hindu and Muslim communities, and journalists attended the Shraddha ceremony at the family’s residence.
Meanwhile, Rangpur Zilla School held a prayer and remembrance meeting Tuesday afternoon in memory of Ganapati and his son Priyam.
Headteacher Abul Kalam Azad, former teacher Shafiar Rahman, former and current students, and hundreds of teachers and students attended the meeting.
They expressed deep grief over the deaths and prayed for the peace of the victims’ souls.
Participants also demanded that the circumstances surrounding the killings be fully uncovered and all those responsible identified and brought to justice.

Golam Parwar: No scope for provocation during Dhaka-Chittagong long march
item.description:
The Dhaka-Chittagong long march to be organized by the opposition Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami-led 11-party alliance on September 5 will be made successful without giving any scope for provocation, Jamaat Secretary General Mia Golam Parwar said Tuesday.
“This is a peaceful and systematic political program. The country’s people will make this long march program a success, InshaAllah, without giving any scope for provocation,” he said at a press briefing at the Jamaat central office in the city.
The 11-party alliance is going to organize the long march with a six-point demand including implementation of the public verdict reflected in the referendum, trial of the July mass killings, resolution of the energy and fertiliser crises, control of prices of essential commodities, improvement of the law-and-order situation, and an end to politicisation at all levels of the administration, he said.
Jamaat Ameer and opposition leader Dr Shafiqur Rahman along with other top leaders of the 11-party alliance will lead the long march, said Golam Parwar.
“We are moving ahead with extensive preparations. We are witnessing a strong response, enthusiasm and excitement among the people (over the programme),” said the Jamaat secretary general.
He said the long march will begin from Shapla Chattar in Dhaka at 7am on September 5 and end at the historic Laldighi Maidan in Chittagong.
Roadside rallies would be held at various important points along the Dhaka-Chittagong Highway during the journey, he added.
Parwar said they expect that more than 1,000 vehicles will participate in the long march, while leaders and activists of the alliance and common people from different districts, upazilas and metropolitan areas along the Dhaka-Chittagong route will join the program.
He said the 11-party alliance held a meeting with the police administration on Monday evening to ensure that the long march remained peaceful and disciplined.
“We informed the police administration about the relevant route, roadside rallies and different spots of the program,” he said.
The Jamaat general secretary said precautionary measures are being taken to minimize disruption to the movement of common people.
“We have planned to keep the long-march convoy on one part of the highway so that regular vehicles can continue to use the other part,” he said.
“However, such a large program may cause temporary inconvenience at some places. So, we apologize to the country’s people in advance,” he added.
Parwar said they are seeking cooperation of the administration, political parties, the media and people from all walks of life to make the program successful.
Jamaat Assistant Secretary General AHM Hamidur Rahman Azad, Dhaka city South unit Ameer Nurul Islam Bulbul and Dhaka city North unit Ameer Md Selim Uddin, among others, were present at the briefing.

item.title: Attack on DMCH physician : Food deliveryman placed on remand
item.description:
A Dhaka court on Tuesday placed food deliveryman Jibon alias Adil on a five-day remand in a case filed over an attack on Dr Mohammad Asadur Rahman, head of the ENT department at Dhaka Medical College Hospital (DMCH).
Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Hasan Shahadat passed the order following a plea by the case’s investigating officer. SI Rokonuzzaman of the prosecution department confirmed the matter.
Asadur Rahman was attacked around 11pm on August 17 in the capital’s Shantinagar area after leaving his chamber at Popular Diagnostic Centre and getting into an autorickshaw.
He suffered injuries to his head, face and eyes and was taken to DMCH, where he is undergoing treatment.
Jibon was detained at the scene and sent to jail the following day. On August 19, Paltan Model Police Station SI Md Atikuzzaman, the investigating officer, sought a 10-day remand for him.
During Tuesday’s hearing, Dhaka Metropolitan Public Prosecutor Omar Faruk Faruqi argued for the remand and sought the maximum period. Jibon had no lawyer.
Asked by the judge if he had anything to say, Jibon said he had gone to see a doctor and that the incident occurred there. He identified himself as a food deliveryman.
He also claimed that several guards at the scene had beaten and injured him, but said he did not know their names.
The court subsequently granted his five-day remand.
Another accused, Farhan Shahriar Evan, was placed on a five-day remand in the case on Saturday.
Asadur Rahman said he had received an extortion demand from an unknown number 11 days before the attack, with a deadline for payment. The attack occurred two days after the deadline expired.
He filed the case with Paltan Police Station on August 18.

item.title: Shama: Govt won’t allow politically motivated detention
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed has said the government will not allow anyone to remain in jail or detention because of political vendetta, regardless of their political affiliation.
“Whether it is the opposition, the Awami League or any other party, the current government will ensure that no one remains unjustly imprisoned or detained because of political vengeance,” she told journalists at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Tuesday.
Her remarks came after Human Rights Watch (HRW) recently called on Bangladesh to end the indefinite pretrial detention of political opponents, noting that the BNP government had promised reforms.
Shama said the government was committed to protecting the human rights of all citizens and would not allow a return to the practices of the previous regime.
“The kind of human rights violations that took place in Bangladesh over the past 17 years had never occurred before in the country's history,” she said.
She said the BNP and its leaders and activists were among the biggest victims of those violations.
“Therefore, we would never want our past fascist era to return, either now or in the future. We want everyone's basic human rights to be ensured and the rights of every citizen to be protected,” she said.
The state minister said a number of cases were filed following the incidents of July-August and the uprising, including cases against those involved in killings and those who allegedly ordered enforced disappearances and killings.
“The cases that were legally supposed to be filed were filed,” she said.
However, she acknowledged that some cases had also been filed “out of excessive enthusiasm.”
The Ministry of Law has said it would review those cases, she added.
“If no truth is found or there is no basis after reviewing the cases, action will be taken accordingly,” Shama said.
She said the government's position was clear: it was committed to protecting human rights and remained accountable to the people.
“Whether it is an opposition party, the Awami League or any other party, the current government will certainly ensure that no one remains unjustly imprisoned or detained because of political vengeance,” she reiterated.

item.title: Miller: Bangladesh likely to join top 30 economies by 2030
item.description:
European Union Ambassador to Bangladesh Michael Miller has said Bangladesh is one of the world’s most dynamic economies and is likely to join the ranks of the world’s 30 largest economies by 2030 or shortly thereafter.
“You are one of the world’s most dynamic economies,” he said. “And I think if you look at the statistics, you’ll know that by 2030, certainly very shortly thereafter if not before, you will be amongst the biggest 30 economies in the entire world. So we know you have this potential.”
Miller made the remarks at a dialogue titled “Meet the Ambassador: Talking Diplomacy for Cooperation” at the Professor Mozaffar Ahmed Chowdhury Auditorium of Dhaka University on Tuesday.
The event was jointly organized by the Centre for Governance Studies (CGS) and Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung Bangladesh.
Miller said the EU recognized Bangladesh’s resilience and economic potential, but noted that European investment in the country remained modest compared with the scale of opportunity.
“Why then, we should ask ourselves, is investment from the EU still rather modest in scale compared to the opportunity that I have just marked out? We think that should change,” he said.
He said the EU was Bangladesh’s largest single source of foreign direct investment, but the volume remained below the level needed to fully support the country’s economic potential.
European companies, he said, could bring technology, standards, innovation and long-term capital to sectors such as energy, transport, water, digital services, health, education, logistics and manufacturing.
However, Miller said Bangladesh would need to strengthen investor confidence by ensuring transparency, policy predictability, regulatory clarity and a level playing field.
He said these measures would help create a more attractive environment for European businesses and encourage greater investment in Bangladesh.
Dhaka University Vice-Chancellor Professor ABM Obaidul Islam, Dean of the Faculty of Social Sciences Professor Kazi Mohammad Mahbobor Rahman and CGS Chairman Zillur Rahman attended the event, along with teachers, students and invited guests.
In his remarks, the vice-chancellor called for stronger Bangladesh-EU cooperation in education, research, technology, climate, trade, human rights, governance and economic development.
He said diplomacy was not confined to government offices or international organizations but was directly linked to the lives and futures of younger generations.
Obaidul Islam also called for more opportunities for students to engage directly with diplomats and discuss international relations and global affairs.
Such initiatives, he said, would help students develop a global outlook, critical thinking and a sense of responsible citizenship.

item.title: Dengue: Death toll 88 as three die in 24 hours
item.description:
Health officials said three more people died of dengue and 907 new cases were recorded across the country in the past 24 hours.
Of the 907 new patients, 163 were hospitalized in Barisal division, 99 in Chittagong division, 49 in Dhaka division, 168 in Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) areas and 88 in Dhaka North City Corporation (DNCC) areas, according to a Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) statement.
The statement said 202 patients were hospitalized in Khulna division, 45 in Mymensingh division, 73 in Rajshahi division, 19 in Rangpur division and one in Sylhet division.
So far this year, 88 people have died of dengue, and 30,830 have been infected, according to the DGHS.
Last year, dengue claimed 413 lives and infected 102,861 people in the country.
In 2024, the disease claimed 575 lives and infected 101,214 people.

item.title: PM greets Muslim Ummah on Eid-e-Miladunnabi
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Tuesday extended greetings and best wishes to Muslims in Bangladesh and around the world on the occasion of Eid-e-Miladunnabi (PBUH).
In a message issued ahead of the occasion, he said the arrival of Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH), the Holy Prophet and Messenger of Allah, was a glorious event in human history.
He said the Prophet (PBUH) called people towards Tawhid and taught truth, justice, equality, brotherhood, humanity and peace, adding that his life and teachings remain an eternal guide for mankind.
Quoting the Holy Quran (Surah Al-Ahzab, verse 21), Tarique Rahman said: “Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah you have a good example to follow.”
The prime minister said the Prophet’s life embodied truthfulness, justice, forgiveness, tolerance, kindness and altruism, while upholding the dignity and rights of all people regardless of race, color, tribe, language or social status.
He said the Prophet’s teachings on peace, justice, compassion and humanity remain highly relevant as the world faces war, conflict, violence, discrimination, intolerance and moral degradation.
Tarique Rahman said following the Prophet’s life and philosophy could help build a peaceful and welfare-oriented society based on justice, responsibility and human values.
Referring to the young generation as the country’s future, he said the Prophet’s ideals could inspire young people to stay away from drugs, terrorism, extremism and crime and remain steadfast on the path of truth and justice.
The prime minister prayed to Almighty Allah to grant all the ability to follow the life and Sunnah of Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH) and to establish peace, justice, equality, prosperity and humanity in Bangladesh and across the world.

item.title: President greets Muslims on Eid-e-Miladunnabi
item.description:
President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir on Tuesday extended heartfelt greetings and Mubarakbad to the people of Bangladesh and Muslims across the world on the occasion of holy Eid-e-Miladunnabi, which will be observed on Wednesday.
In a message, the head of State described the advent of Prophet Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH) as the greatest and most epoch-making event in human history.
He said the Prophet (PBUH) emerged as a messenger of welfare and salvation for all humanity in this world and the hereafter.
The Holy Quran, a complete code of life and guidance for humankind, was revealed to him, while Islam was established as a religion of peace based on equality, brotherhood and humanity, said Mirza Fakhrul.
The president said Prophet Muhammad (PBUH), through his life and deeds, set an unparalleled example of truth, justice, forgiveness, compassion and human dignity. He upheld the rights of orphans, the poor, the helpless and the deprived, while providing clear guidance on the rights of women, children, neighbours and working people.
He said the lessons of human dignity, rights, equality, justice and mutual responsibility that the Prophet (PBUH) conveyed in his Farewell Hajj (last sermon) remain universal and should always be followed by humanity.
The president observed that the Prophet’s (PBUH) ideals of peace, justice, tolerance, love and humanity are even more relevant in today’s world, which is beset by wars, conflicts, violence, discrimination and intolerance.
He called upon all to draw inspiration from the life and teachings of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH), shun hatred, hostility, division and injustice, and pledge to build a just society and state based on peace, harmony, equality and humanity.
President Mirza Fakhrul prayed to Almighty Allah for His mercy, blessings, peace and welfare upon Bangladesh and people across the world. He also prayed for divine guidance to enable all to follow the life and teachings of Prophet Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH).

item.title: Trump says executions of Iran protesters must stop
item.description:
US President Donald Trump expressed outrage on Tuesday at the mounting number of executions in Iran of people allegedly involved in mass protests earlier this year before the Middle East war began.
“The failing Islamic Republic of Iran is not paying large segments of their military, while at the same time killing protesters, even when they are not protesting, at levels not seen before,” he wrote on Truth Social.
“It is a humanitarian crisis of epic proportions, and must be stopped, NOW,” he added.
It was not immediately clear what new information had spurred the early morning post, but there has been a steady increase in executions since the outbreak of the war on February 28.
The joint US-Israeli strikes which kicked off the war came weeks after the violent quelling of mass protests in Iran.
Rallies initially began in late December over outrage at the high cost of living, but rapidly evolved into widespread anti-government demonstrations that peaked on January 8 and 9.
Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths, but attributed the violence to “terrorist acts” orchestrated by the United States and Israel.
Rights groups based abroad recorded a far higher toll and said the security forces had fired on demonstrators.
Earlier this month, more than 30 countries signed a joint letter condemning “in the strongest terms the ongoing executions of protesters and use of the death penalty” by Iran.
The United States, where capital punishment is still legal, did not sign the letter.
Since then, at least three more people have been executed in Iran on charges related to the protests.

item.title: Netanyahu got his Iran war, but maybe not his desired result
item.description:
After decades of urging the United States to attack Iran, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu finally got his wish. But after six months of inconclusive hostilities, Israel may ultimately find itself in a worse position than it was before the war.
The Islamic republic, which Netanyahu has long cast as an existential threat, has not only survived but appears emboldened.
Underlying Netanyahu’s dilemma have been the wild swings in the approach of US President Donald Trump, who joined Israel in launching the conflict in late February, but by April abruptly called a ceasefire and sought a negotiated settlement in the face of souring public opinion and soaring oil prices.
“It’s a colossal failure of Israeli strategy regarding Iran,” said Danny Citrinowicz, a former top Israeli intelligence analyst on Iran who is now at the Tel Aviv-based Institute for National Security Studies.
“Yes, we had operational achievements, but strategically we’ve failed.”
Israel on the very first day killed Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, the supreme leader who ruthlessly suppressed dissent in Iran, including mass protests earlier this year, and backed virulently anti-Israeli groups like Hamas, which led the October 7, 2023 resistance campaign.
But Khamenei was also seen as holding back on full-blown pursuit of nuclear weapons, a reluctance that could now end if the Islamic republic feels it has lost its conventional deterrents.
While Trump has recently declared economic warfare on Iran and periodically ordered new strikes, he has voiced support for a deal that would see sanctions relief.
Netanyahu had adamantly rejected a 2015 nuclear deal negotiated by then-president Barack Obama.
Citrinowicz said Israel now had a choice between accepting a new nuclear deal that would strengthen Iran, or trying to weaken it further and increasing the risk that it will seek a nuclear weapon.
“Israel is trying to do both but it’s not going to work,” he said.
An extraordinary 92 percent of Israelis believe Iran won or gained more from the conflict, according to a June survey by the Hebrew University of Jerusalem in collaboration with the Agam Institute -- a warning sign for Netanyahu ahead of October 27 elections.
Netanyahu had said he was hoping to “create conditions for regime change” but did not explicitly make toppling the Islamic republic his goal.
Instead, some see Netanyahu following an Israeli playbook witnessed in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria -- inflict overwhelming damage that will allow Israel to return and attack later as it sees fit, a strategy the country euphemistically calls “mowing the grass.”
“Netanyahu doesn’t see this as a loss. He has the United States directly at war with Iran, with Israel for now on the sidelines,” one foreign diplomat based in Israel told AFP on condition of anonymity.
Iranian counter-strikes killed 25 people in Israel and four in the occupied West Bank, but Iran has focused its fire more recently on Gulf Arab states that provide bases for US troops.
Alex Grinberg, a senior fellow focused on Iran at the Turan Research Center, said the war set back Iran significantly by eliminating infrastructure and people in the nuclear program and imposing massive economic damage.
“I think Israel did achieve its strategic goals, meaning denying the Iranian regime the strategic capacity to threaten Israel,” he said, while casting doubt on the prospects for a favourable US-Iran deal.
The war has already complicated Israel’s relationship with its most crucial ally, and may preclude any possibility of a future reconciliation with the Iranian people.
The increasingly unpopular conflict triggered a surge of criticism of Israel in the United States, where its war against Hamas in Gaza had already dealt a heavy blow to its standing in the public eye.
Public perceptions of Israel inside Iran are difficult to gauge, as polling is difficult, but the two countries were allies before the Islamic revolution, and protests before the war indicated noticeable public opposition to the clerical government.
And while Netanyahu and Trump have both publicly professed to support the Iranian people, the US and Israel have issued apocalyptic threats over the course of the war that appeared to make little distinction between the Islamic republic and its citizens, and their strikes have destroyed infrastructure including top universities.
There is “a real possibility of lasting hostility towards Israel and the United States, particularly if the war is remembered through civilian casualties and damage to the country rather than solely through the removal of senior regime figures”, said Liora Hendelman-Baavur, a senior research fellow at the Alliance Center for Iranian Studies at Tel Aviv University.
“That hostility would not necessarily restore the Islamic republic’s legitimacy, but it could complicate future relations long after the present leadership has changed.”

item.title: Trees are vital for cooler cities, but they need help too
item.description:
Walking beneath the trees this historically hot summer, sometimes felt like autumn had already arrived: dry, dead leaves crunching underfoot, and crowns tinged yellow or completely bare.
That’s a problem because large leafy trees help make our cities more livable. They block sunlight, reduce pollution, store carbon, provide habitats for biodiversity to thrive, soak up otherwise harmful stormwater runoff and even boost the mental and physical health of residents.
“When trees go away, those things go away as well,” Nina Bassuk, who runs the Urban Horticulture Institute at the US-based Cornell University, told DW.
That’s why cities and scientists are racing to figure out how to save trees and choose smarter ones for the future.
As humans have burned fossil fuels to power industry and heat homes, the planet has become hotter, making the role of urban trees ever more vital.
Why? Because they essentially act like giant air conditioners, which makes a big difference in hot cities. Inside a tree’s canopy, temperatures can be up to three degrees cooler than the surrounding area. This is down to evapotranspiration, the process of trees absorbing water and releasing water vapor through their leaves.
In addition, trees cast shade, which keeps their surroundings from heating up in the first place.
“When we stand under a tree, the temperature we perceive can be 10 to 12 degrees Celsius (18 to 22 degrees Fahrenheit) lower than right next to it,” said Matthias Beyer, a hydrologist at the Institute of Geoecology at TU Braunschweig.
And it’s not just cooling. There have been numerous studies correlating all sorts of other positive effects of robust trees.
One showed that cities with more tree canopy had lower rates of cardiovascular disease. Another concluded that greener school surroundings were associated with better grades in high schools. And further research suggested that more greenspace exposure during pregnancy can lead to healthier outcomes for newborns.”
Though a warmer climate makes trees more necessary, it also makes it harder for them to thrive.
Healthy trees need a minimum of 10 to 15 liters of water a day, but mature ones with full foliage require up to four times that.
While there may be a temptation for cities to focus on planting new, less water-hungry trees, experts agree that the priority should be protecting older, struggling ones.
Research shows it would take around 400 saplings to replace the benefits of an old tree with a crown circumference of 20 meters. Once trees reach maturation, their benefits can be exponential, but this takes time and lots of maintenance.
“A lot of trees can’t deliver the full function until 40, 50 years from the day they were planted,” said Henrik Sjoman, a researcher at the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences.
It’s better to give trees a large amount of water over a short period so it can soak down deep, rather than letting it stay in the upper soil layers, where much of it evaporates.
For newly planted trees, a ring of metal or sturdy plastic is often fixed into the ground around the trunk. Where that’s not available, a shallow depression around the tree can be created, allowing the water to pool. What matters is not damaging any surface roots in the process.
When the soil is extremely hardened, so-called irrigation bags or cushions can help. Water drips slowly but steadily into the soil through small holes on their underside. The water mustn’t sit on the surface for long periods, since that can cause rot, which damages the tree.
But sometimes the soil has been heavily compacted to support sidewalks above, meaning water can’t get through at all. Thirty years ago, Bassuk helped pioneer a method that mixes specially sized gravel in with the soil. It lets the stones bear the load of the sidewalk, while leaving more space for roots to stretch across dense urban ground.
“As long as you get the soil and the stone proportions right, you can compact it and yet trees can access that and grow for long distances,” Bassuk said.
When it comes to climate adaptation, there’s also the question of which trees to plant in the first place.
Historically, Sjoman says urban tree selection was often driven by aesthetics and design, which led to the over-planting of single species that were vulnerable to threats like pests or disease. Horror stories of Dutch elm disease wiping out entire populations in the 20th century helped to transform urban forestry planning, placing the focus far more on diversity and climate adaptation.
The 10-20-30 rule of thumb was coined in 1990 by the late Frank Santamour, who worked as a research geneticist at the US National Arboretum. It states that urban forest populations should include no more than 10% of any one species, 20% of a single genus or 30% of any family.
In Germany, there are several tools and databases that offer planting guidance, and several cities are taking part in an official street tree test. The idea is that 45 species are tested at more than 220 locations to gather knowledge of how they thrive.
Another resource is the CITREE database, which categorizes almost 400 species of woody plants, sortable by more than 50 different features, including leaf density, fruit color, allergy potential, limb breakage and more.
The key feature cities need to select is drought tolerance — considering the immense biological strain urban
trees are facing in an ever-warming world. But knowing the benefits trees offer a city means that is not the only factor.
“The demands of trees today — it’s so much bigger, so much deeper than it was just a couple of decades ago,” Sjoman said.

Canada to unveil response to Trump's steep tariffs
item.description:
Canada is due to announce its answer to US President Donald Trump's latest wave of tariffs Tuesday, as a trade war intensifies between the historically close allies.

The new measures aim to support workers and businesses during "challenging times," Canada's government said late Monday, with officials to hold a press briefing to detail Ottawa's response Tuesday morning.

Fresh 50-per cent US tariffs took effect on a range of Canadian goods Saturday, after trade negotiations collapsed the prior day at the eleventh hour.

The duties impact some $20 billion in goods, or about 5.5 per cent of Canadian exports to the United States, economists estimate.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said retaliatory tariffs would be effective 8 September, as analysts warn of tit-for-tat escalation.

On Monday, Trump additionally pledged to double tariffs on Canadian autos starting next year, up to 50 per cent from the current 25 per cent for non-US content.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford criticised Trump's tariff threat on autos, saying he could "kiss my ass" and threatening an electricity export surcharge.

In an earlier phase of the dispute, Ontario imposed a temporary 25-per cent surcharge on electricity exports to three US states.

Trump has since lashed out at Ford online, warning of "far worse" consequences.

He also referred to the Canadian prime minister as a "governor," re-upping his inflammatory push for Canada to become the 51st US state.

Highlighting the animosity, Trump on Tuesday said he was considering renaming Lake Ontario as "Lake America," as he did last year with the Gulf of Mexico.

The latest tariffs Trump imposed will raise the US effective tariff rate on Canadian exports to 6.9 per cent from 5.1 per cent, Oxford Economics estimates.

Tariffs on plastics, electrical machinery, and wood and paper products contribute the most to the increase.

"Manufacturers in Quebec, New Brunswick, and Ontario will be affected the most," Oxford Economics said.

Threats to culture

Over the weekend, Carney said US negotiators had sought restrictions on Canadian trade deals with other countries at the last minute.

US officials made unacceptable "threats" to the French language and "Quebec culture" too, he added, referring to eastern Canada's French-speaking province.

But Trump pushed back early Tuesday, saying on his Truth Social platform that he would "never interfere with Canadians speaking French!"

"This lie was made up by a weak and ineffective Prime Minister in an attempt to gain political support," Trump charged.

The United States is by far Canada's biggest trading partner, with Canadian exports to its neighbour representing 70 per cent of its overall total.

Canada is the United States' second biggest trading partner in goods this year, behind Mexico, government data showed.

Polling released Sunday by the Angus Reid Institute showed Canadian broadly support Carney's move to walk away from talks, but some have fear of economic repercussions.

The White House had alleged "discriminatory treatment" by Canada against US alcohol, automobile and dairy products in rolling out the 50-per cent tariffs.

Trump had delayed their implementation, but both sides failed to reach an agreement after talks went down to the wire.

Besides the tariffs fight, Washington and Ottawa have to agree on revisions to the US-Mexico-Canada free trade agreement (USMCA) which Trump has declined to renew in its current form.

item.title: Boat carrying four members of New Zealand family capsizes in Cox’s Bazar, one missing
item.description:
A wooden boat carrying four members of a New Zealand family capsized at the mouth of the Sonadia Channel in the Bay of Bengal off the Cox’s Bazar coast on Tuesday morning.

Three of the foreigners, including two women, were rescued by local fishermen, but a 16-year-old boy from the family remains missing. A search operation continued until 5:00pm, but the teenager could not be found. The Coast Guard and Fire Service are conducting the search in the Maheshkhali Channel.

Confirming the incident, Sheikh Mohammad Ali, officer-in-charge of Cox’s Bazar Sadar Model Police Station, told Prothom Alo that the four-member New Zealand family had set out from the Nazirartek coast at around 9:15am on a wooden boat to cross the sea channel to Sonadia Island in Maheshkhali. When the boat reached the middle of the channel, it began rocking heavily after being hit by large waves. At one point, a wave overturned the boat, throwing all four foreigners into the water.

Fishermen aboard nearby fishing boats rushed to the scene and rescued three people, including two women. However, the teenage member of the family could not be found until 5:00pm. Coast Guard and Fire Service teams are searching the channel for him. The three rescued foreigners are receiving treatment at a hospital. The family had been staying in Cox’s Bazar, the OC said.

According to information provided by police and the Fire Service, the missing teenager has been identified as Albert, 16. The three people rescued alive are Edward, 74, Bella, 36, and Ralph, 13. Local fishermen rescued the three and handed them over to the Coast Guard.

Two fishermen from the Nazirartek area said members of the New Zealand family had been travelling around Cox’s Bazar, Maheshkhali and Sonadia for several days. On Tuesday morning, they went out to sea from the Nazirartek coast on a wooden boat. When they reached the Sonadia estuary area of the Maheshkhali Channel, the boat sank after being hit by a large wave, throwing all four into the water.

Local fishermen who were nearby witnessed the accident and immediately rushed to the scene. Their efforts enabled three people to be rescued. After being informed of the incident, Coast Guard and Fire Service personnel arrived and began searching for the missing teenager.

Dolon Acharya, senior station officer at the Cox’s Bazar Fire Service Station, said a specialised Fire Service team reached the scene soon after receiving the news of the accident and began the rescue operation. A team of divers is searching for the missing teenager. The three rescued people are receiving first aid, he said.

item.title: Japanese firm bids to operate Dhaka Airport third terminal
item.description:
A Japanese company has submitted a proposal to operate and maintain the third terminal of Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport.
Representatives of Sub Working Group submitted the proposal to the Bangladesh Civil Aviation Authority (CAAB) at its headquarters on Tuesday, said CAAB spokesperson Kawsar Mahmud.
He said Masahiru Hirai, representing the Japanese company, handed over the proposal to CAAB Chairman Air Vice Marshal Md Mostafa Mahmud Siddiq.
Other CAAB members and representatives of the Japanese delegation were also present.
The company submitted separate technical and financial proposals as part of the process.
The proposals will be evaluated by an RFP Evaluation Committee formed by the Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism.
The committee includes representatives from CAAB, the Ministry of Finance, the Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism, the Prime Minister’s Office, the Public Private Partnership (PPP) Authority and the Roads and Highways Department.
Under the evaluation process, the technical proposal will be assessed first, followed by the financial proposal.
After the evaluation, the authorities will hold necessary discussions and negotiations with the company. Once the negotiations are successfully completed, the contract date will be finalized following the prescribed procedure.
The third terminal is one of the country's largest and most important aviation infrastructure projects.
The project is expected to strengthen Bangladesh's aviation sector through modern technology, international-standard passenger services and more efficient operational management.

HC directs officials to stop displaying flags behind chairs
item.description:
The High Court on Tuesday directed officials and employees of government and autonomous institutions to refrain from unlawfully displaying the national flag behind their chairs or sofas.
The bench of Justice Ahmed Sohel and Justice S M Iftekhar Uddin Mahmud issued the order, along with a rule, in response to a writ petition challenging the practice.
Lawyer Sharif Sarkar filed the writ while H M Shanjid Siddique represented the petitioner during the hearing.
Shanjid said officials at various government offices have recently been displaying the national flag behind their desks or chairs while sitting in front of it, which he said is not permitted under the law.
He said the National Flag Rules, 1972 allow 15 categories of people to use the national flag at their offices, residences and vehicles, but do not permit officials to display it permanently behind their chairs.
The lawyer also said the rules require the national flag displayed on a building to be flown from sunrise to sunset and remain free-floating. However, the flags placed behind officials’ chairs are often bent or curved rather than properly flown.
The court’s rule asked why displaying the national flag behind officials or chairs in such a manner should not be declared illegal. In its interim order, the court directed officials and employees of government and autonomous institutions to refrain from unlawfully displaying the national flag beside or behind their chairs or sofas.
The court also directed the Cabinet Secretary to form a three-member committee comprising a judicial officer, a representative of the Cabinet Division and a teacher from a public university.
The committee has been asked to submit a report within 60 days on whether national flags displayed in government offices are being used in accordance with the National Flag Rules.

item.title: Gold chain snatched from 4-year-old girl at knifepoint in Rangpur
item.description:
Two men on a motorcycle allegedly stopped an autorickshaw in Pirganj, Rangpur, and snatched a gold chain from a four-year-old girl after holding a knife to her throat on Monday afternoon.
The incident occurred around 4:00pm near the Pirganj Fire Station in Mokimpur area. Shamima Akter, an assistant teacher at Mokimpur Government Primary School, said she was returning home with a colleague when the men intercepted their autorickshaw.
They allegedly held a knife to the throat of Shamima’s four-year-old daughter, Taisha Jannat, and threatened to kill her unless they handed over their valuables.
As Shamima and her colleague screamed for help, the men allegedly pulled a gold chain from the child’s neck and fled.
The chain weighed about one bhori and one ana and was worth around Tk 250,000, Shamima said.
Pirganj Police Station Officer-in-Charge Nazmul Haque confirmed receiving a written complaint and said police had launched an investigation.
“Necessary legal action will be taken soon,” he said.

item.title: US-Bangla Airlines resumes Dhaka-Jessore flights from Sept 9
item.description:
US-Bangla Airlines will resume flights on the Dhaka-Jessore route from September 9, 2026, in response to long-standing demand from people in Greater Jessore.
The airline will operate two round-trip flights a day on Saturday, Wednesday and Thursday using its 72-seat ATR 72-600 aircraft.
Under the new schedule, the first flight will leave Dhaka at 9:30am and arrive in Jessore at 10:15am. The return flight will depart Jessore at 10:45am and reach Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka at 11:30am.
The second flight will depart Dhaka at 4:45pm and arrive in Jessore at 5:30pm. The return flight will leave Jessore at 6pm and arrive in Dhaka at 6:45pm.
The minimum one-way fare has been set at Tk5,749, while the minimum return fare will be Tk11,498. All applicable taxes and surcharges are included in the fares.
US-Bangla Airlines began operations on July 17, 2014, with its first flight on the Dhaka-Jessore route. Since then, the airline has focused on expanding domestic air connectivity and providing faster and more convenient travel between Dhaka and different parts of the country.
At present, US-Bangla operates regular domestic flights from Dhaka to Cox’s Bazar, Chittagong, Sylhet, Saidpur and Rajshahi.
The resumption of the Dhaka-Jessore route is aimed at meeting the transportation needs of people in Greater Jessore. The renewed connectivity is expected to facilitate travel for business, education, medical treatment, tourism and other essential purposes, while contributing to the region’s economic and commercial activities.
The airline said it would continue to monitor passenger demand and market conditions and may consider increasing the frequency of flights on the route in the future, subject to operational feasibility.

item.title: Kit Harington joins Harry Potter series as Gilderoy Lockhart
item.description:
“Game of Thrones” star Kit Harington has been cast as Gilderoy Lockhart in the second season of HBO’s “Harry Potter” series, replacing Nicholas Hoult, who left the production due to scheduling conflicts.
The casting was confirmed by the official Harry Potter social media account on August 24. Hoult had been announced for the role earlier this month.
According to Deadline, Hoult’s existing commitments created scheduling conflicts with the series. He is also set to reprise his role as Lex Luthor in the upcoming Superman sequel “Man of Tomorrow."
Harington has previously voiced Lockhart in Audible’s “Harry Potter: The Full-Cast Audio Editions” of “Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets," released in 2025.

item.title: ‘You'll write, and we'll beat you up', says BNP leader after assaulting 3 journalists
item.description:
Three journalists from Shariatpur have reportedly been assaulted by Arifuzzaman Molla, the Joint General Secretary of the district BNP.

When contacted over the phone for comments on the incident, he allegedly threatened another journalist, saying, "You will write, and we will beat."

On Tuesday morning, journalists Zahid Hasan from The Daily Star, Bidhan Majumdar from News 24 Television and Jago News, and Barkat Molla, the district correspondent for Manabkantha, were beaten when they went to the district administrator's office campus.

At that time, BNP leaders from Shariatpur were holding a protest rally there.

In an attempt to learn why the journalists were attacked, Palash Khan, President of the Jazira Upazila Press Club and Shariatpur correspondent for Sonali News, called BNP leader Arifuzzaman Molla in the afternoon.

Arifuzzaman Molla said, "I have beaten more people, not just now, they can file complaints against me. Many are on the list. Insha''Allah, by God's grace, you will hear more news this evening. Be prepared yourself. Where are you now? Sit tight, I am coming. Many people have said many things, you have also said a lot, that Bashar said things, Rajib said things. . . . You write, we will beat. Not for nothing, my point is, you called me, check your RS and CS."

Regarding this, journalist Palash Khan told Prothom Alo, "While fulfilling their professional duties, our three colleagues were attacked and beaten, allegedly by BNP leader Arif Molla. I called his phone to get his statement regarding this. When I inquired about the incident, he threatened to assault me and my colleagues too. He also made derogatory comments about the press club and its president and secretary general. I have verbally informed the police about this and will take legal action in writing."

Attempts to contact district BNP's Joint General Secretary Arifuzzaman Molla for his statement on the matter were made several times until 8 PM on Tuesday, but he did not answer the calls.

Additional Superintendent of Police for Shariatpur (Naria and Sadar Circle), Muhammad Mohiuddin Miraj, said, "We have learned about the attack on journalists. We have not yet received any written complaints. Legal action will be taken upon receiving a written complaint."

Several journalists in the district town reported that on Saturday night, three walls of the press club’s boundary were demolished under an initiative by the Shariatpur district administration.

Protesting this incident, journalist BM Israfil made a post on social media with images of the press club president Abul Hossain and district administrator Tahsina Begum. As a consequence of that post, he was attacked.

In protest of the attack and the demolition of the press club's boundary walls, journalists working in Shariatpur organised a protest march and human chain programme in front of the district administrator's office on Sunday afternoon, demanding the withdrawal of the district administrator. This led to a faction of the local BNP being angered with the journalists. They organised a protest and rally today.

Under the banner of “All Levels of Shariatpur District People,” the district level BNP leaders were also present in the programme.

Around 10: 30 in the morning, when BNP leaders, activists, and supporters were gathering in front of the district administrator's office, journalists Zahid Hasan, Bidhan Majumdar, and Barkat Molla went there and were attacked under the leadership of Arifuzzaman Molla.

item.title: 202 dengue patients hospitalized in Khulna division in 24 hours
item.description:
A total of 202 new dengue patients were admitted to hospitals across Khulna division in the past 24 hours, raising the number of patients currently undergoing treatment to 618.
The information was disclosed in a report issued by the office of the Divisional Director of Health.
According to the report, a total of 4,806 dengue patients have been hospitalized across the division since January 1 this year. Of them, 16 have died, while 4,089 patients have recovered and been discharged. So far, 83 patients have been referred to other hospitals.
Divisional Director of Health Dr Sheikh Md Mosharraf Hossain said that of the 202 new patients admitted in the past 24 hours, 156 were admitted to government hospitals and 46 to private hospitals.
The data showed that 87 new dengue patients were admitted in Khulna district during the period. Another 56 patients were admitted to Khulna Medical College Hospital. In addition, 14 patients were admitted in Bagerhat, 17 in Jessore, two in Satkhira, two at Satkhira Medical College Hospital, four in Magura, 13 in Narail, two in Kushtia, three in Chuadanga and two in Meherpur.
Currently, 255 dengue patients are undergoing treatment in hospitals in Khulna, while 156 are at Khulna Medical College Hospital. item.title: Moyeen: Danish support can help address Dhaka's water crisis
item.description:
Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives Minister Dr Abdul Moyeen Khan on Tuesday said Denmark's cooperation can play an important role in addressing the capital's growing demand for safe drinking water and worsening water crisis.
Denmark can be an important partner of Bangladesh in the fields of water supply, waste management and development assistance, he said when Danish Ambassador to Bangladesh Christian Brix Moller called on him at the Secretariat.
During the meeting, they discussed strengthening bilateral relations between Bangladesh and Denmark, expanding cooperation in water supply and waste management, and the possibility of Danish investment in development projects.
At the onset of the meeting, the Danish envoy congratulated the Bangladesh minister on assuming his new responsibility.
At the same time, he hoped that bilateral relations would be strengthened between Bangladesh and Denmark in the future, while the areas of cooperation would be expanded.
The minister said Denmark can play an important role in key sectors such as water supply and waste management in Bangladesh. "Especially, Denmark has investment opportunities in producing energy from waste," he said.
They also discussed various aspects of Denmark's financing and cooperation in the Sayedabad Water Treatment Plant Project (Phase-3).
The Danish government will finance Tk 4,500 crore in the project. Of the amount, Tk 1,500 crore will be given in grants and Tk 3,000 crore in soft loans.
After the meeting, State Minister for LGRD and Cooperatives Mir Shahe Alam told reporters that Denmark's support in the third phase of the Sayedabad Water Treatment Plant Project is a big success for the government. "Once the project is implemented, it will be possible to meet the increasing demand for clean water in Dhaka to a great extent," he added.

Holy Eid-e-Miladunnabi tomorrow
item.description:
The holy Eid-e-Miladunnabi, commemorating the birth and death anniversary of Prophet Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH) will be observed across the country tomorrow with due religious solemnity.

On the 12th of Rabiul Awal (in 570 AD), Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) was born in Makkah, bringing divine blessings and a message of peace for mankind. He passed away on the same day (in 632 AD).

The day is a national holiday.

The government has taken extensive national-level programmes to mark the day.

On the occasion, President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir and Prime Minister Tarique Rahman issued separate messages greeting Muslims across the world.

Besides, the president has inaugurated the Islamic Foundation''s fortnight programme titled ''Siratunnabi (PBUH) Programme'' at the Baitul Mukarram National Mosque here this evening.

According to the government''s national programme, the national flag will be hoisted at all government, semi-government, autonomous institutions, private establishments and armed forces installations tomorrow.

Special prayers will be offered at mosques across the country, including the Bangladesh Secretariat Mosque.

Bangladesh missions abroad will also observe the day with due respect. Relevant ministries and departments have been instructed to take special measures to maintain peace and law and order during the observance.
The Islamic Foundation has chalked out several progammes from 25 August to 8 September.

The events include Islamic sermons, seminars and discussions, alongside competitions in qirat, hamd-naat, recitation of self-composed poems and Arabic essay writing.

The foundation will also host an Islamic cultural competition with participation of school, college, university and madrasah students, calligraphy exhibition, and month-long Islamic book fair and publish Sirat souvenirs and supplementary materials.

The fair will be organized in the east and south courtyards of the National Mosque Baitul Mukarram.

According to the Islamic Foundation, renowned Islamic scholars of the country will deliver sermons every day from after Maghrib to 10:00pm during the fortnight programme.

These events will emphasize establishing a spirit of morality, humanity, tolerance and peace in individual, family and social life by following the ideals and Sunnah of Prophet Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH).

In honor of the Prophet (PBUH), the Islamic Foundation and Bangladesh Betar will jointly host a seminar while Bangladesh Betar will broadcast a poetry recitation event.

Divisional, district and upazila administrations, city corporations, municipalities and the armed forces will organise discussions and doa mahfils in their respective jurisdictions.

Bangladesh Television, Bangladesh Betar and other electronic media have been requested to broadcast special programmes while newspapers will publish supplements on the occasion.

All the relevant organisations will organise discussions, doa mahfils, hamd-naat, poetry recitations, cultural and quiz competitions focusing on the life and teachings of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH), and on Islam's message of peace, progress, fraternity, patience, human rights and women''s dignity.

Bangladesh Shishu Academy will arrange special programmes for children, including hamd-naat, discussions and essay competitions.

Important road islands, light posts, and major city points will be decorated with national and colorful flags, along with banners inscribed with the Kalima Tayyiba to mark the day.

Improved diets will be served at all military and civil hospitals, prisons, government orphanages, child development centers, and old-age homes.

item.title: Fertilizer crisis: What is driving shortages and price hikes?
item.description:
For farmers preparing their fields for the winter crop season, fertilizer has become a growing source of concern, with many saying they are struggling to find government-priced supplies despite repeated assurances from the authorities that there is no nationwide shortage.
Mokbul Hossain (not his real name), a farmer from a southwestern district, recently bought diammonium phosphate (DAP), muriate of potash (MOP), triple super phosphate (TSP) and urea from a local vendor at prices higher than the government-fixed rates.
“I bought fertilizer from the local market to save time and avoid the hassle. DAP is selling at Tk33 per kg, urea at Tk30, MOP at Tk55 and TSP at around Tk50 in our area,” he said.
The government-fixed retail prices, however, are Tk21 per kg for DAP, Tk20 for MOP, Tk27 for TSP and Tk27 for urea.
Mokbul said farmers often face difficulties obtaining fertilizer from dealers even when stocks are available.
“Dealers receive fertilizer according to their allocation and distribution schedule. But some sell fertilizer outside the official distribution system at higher prices. If a dealer receives 500 sacks, farmers may have to wait while only around 200 are actually sold to them, with the rest kept aside or sold elsewhere,” he said.
Similar complaints have emerged from different parts of the country as farmers enter the peak Aman and winter crop seasons.
The situation drew nationwide attention on Sunday when farmers in Kurigram’s Bhurungamari upazila broke into a fertilizer dealer’s warehouse and took away 197 sacks of urea and MOP, alleging an artificial shortage and overcharging.
The incident has brought renewed focus to a central contradiction in the current fertilizer market: the government says there is sufficient fertilizer in the country, yet farmers in several areas say they cannot obtain it at the official price.
At a press briefing on Tuesday, Prime Minister’s Information and Broadcasting Adviser Dr Zahed Ur Rahman said there was no overall shortage of fertilizer and that the government had approved sufficient imports to meet demand.
As of August 24, the country had 1.365 million tonnes of fertilizer in stock, including 482,200 tonnes of urea, 369,000 tonnes of TSP, 368,000 tonnes of DAP and 146,000 tonnes of MOP, according to government figures cited by Zahed. Another 865,000 tonnes was at the import stage.
Zahed acknowledged, however, that temporary problems had emerged in some areas because of disruptions in the distribution system. He also said some dealers had failed to lift their allocated fertilizer, contributing to local shortages.
The government has taken action against some dealers amid allegations of irregularities. Five dealership licences have been suspended and around 25 dealers fined in connection with the recent crisis, according to a report published on Tuesday.
The available information points to four interconnected factors: distribution problems, disputes over the new dealer policy, higher demand and constraints on domestic fertilizer production.
Agriculture Minister Mohammed Aminur Rashid has described the unrest at the field level as a planned conspiracy by dealers, saying they are unhappy with the government’s new fertilizer dealership policy.
Dealers, however, say the problem is more complicated.
Rajshahi fertilizer dealer Osman Mia told Dhaka Tribune that allocations initially fell short of demand, creating a supply gap during the current season.
He said allocations for September had already been released and expressed hope that the situation would improve soon.
Golam Mostofa, a dealer in Kurigram Sadar upazila, said demand had increased because farmers were cultivating more land this year.
“Farmers are cultivating more land this year as there has been no flooding compared with previous years. As a result, demand for fertilizer is also higher,” he said.
Another source of tension is the revised Fertilizer Dealer Appointment and Retention Policy 2025, which brings dealers operating under the Bangladesh Chemical Industries Corporation (BCIC) and the Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation (BADC) under a unified dealership system.
Some dealers claim the changes have created uncertainty over existing dealerships and increased competition within the distribution network.
Ministry sources say some dealers appointed under the previous system fear losing their dealerships under the new criteria. They also point to longstanding tensions between BCIC- and BADC-affiliated dealers.
Officials have also dismissed rumours that retailers will be scrapped altogether under the new policy, saying action will instead be taken against retailers operating without proper licences or trading under someone else’s name.
Such rumours, officials say, have added to uncertainty and instability in the market.
Mohammad Mosharraf Hossain, chairman of the Bangladesh Fertilizer Association, told Dhaka Tribune that dealers are unhappy following the implementation of the new dealership policy.
“Appointing two additional dealers per union, as proposed under the new policy, risks financial harm to both existing and incoming dealers,” he said.
The fertilizer problem is also linked to Bangladesh’s wider gas crisis, which has disrupted domestic production.
Fertilizer factories have been operating below capacity because of inadequate gas supplies, affecting the country’s ability to maintain domestic urea production.
The Ashuganj Fertilizer Factory has remained shut since March 2025, while the Jamuna Fertilizer Company has also been out of operation since February, according to BCIC officials.
In an interview with Dhaka Tribune on Tuesday, Md Moniruzzaman, director (production) of BCIC, said three of the corporation’s five fertilizer factories were currently operating.
The production constraints are particularly significant because Bangladesh remains heavily dependent on imported fertilizer to meet domestic demand.
The government has continued approving fresh imports to maintain supplies. Tuesday, the government approved the procurement of 365,000 tonnes of fertilizer, including urea, MOP, DAP and TSP, through government-to-government arrangements.
The conflicting accounts suggest that the current situation cannot simply be described as either a nationwide fertilizer shortage or no shortage at all.
At the national level, government warehouses have substantial stocks and additional imports are being arranged. But at the local level, farmers say they are facing difficulties obtaining fertilizer on time and at government-fixed prices.
That gap between national stocks and local availability is where distribution irregularities, dealer disputes and increased seasonal demand appear to be converging.
The government has formed a three-member Cabinet committee, headed by Women and Children Affairs and Social Welfare Minister Abu Jafar Md Zahid Hossain, to review the fertilizer situation.
The committee will now face the more immediate question confronting farmers: not simply whether fertilizer exists somewhere in the country, but whether it reaches their fields on time and at the price fixed by the government.

item.title: Who gets to decide what Bangladesh can celebrate?
item.description:
Ali Azmat had already flown into Dhaka. Kaavish had arrived too. Atif Aslam was supposed to follow.
Tickets had been sold, posters circulated and thousands of fans were waiting.
Then the concerts disappeared from the calendar.
In November and December last year, Dhaka witnessed an extraordinary run of cancellations and postponements involving some of South Asia’s biggest performers.
A James-Ali Azmat concert was called off on the day of the show.
Jal’s “Sound of Soul” was postponed after failing to secure government permission.
Kaavish came to Dhaka but could not take the stage.
Anuv Jain’s concert was postponed over security concerns, while Atif Aslam’s much-publicised December show also collapsed amid problems over permissions and clearances.
For audiences, the explanations varied, or were sometimes far from clear.
Security concerns, administrative permission, the political situation and “unavoidable circumstances” repeatedly appeared in cancellation notices.
The uncertainty did not end with the change of year.
Indian singer Anupam Roy’s Dhaka concert was stopped at the last minute in June despite organisers saying preparations and approvals had been completed.
Rescheduled for August 1, it was stopped again, this time after the Cultural Affairs Ministry instructed organizers not to hold the event.
But what initially looked like a problem confined to concerts is increasingly taking on a broader and more troubling character.
In Kishoreganj, an Ashes-led concert lost permission following objections from Islamic scholars.
In Brahmanbaria, a police-organized cultural program descended into clashes after madrasa students objected to music.
A film screening in the same district had earlier been postponed following opposition from a Qawmi student group.
Elsewhere, Lalon programs, Basanta celebrations and other traditional events have faced obstruction.
Now pressure has reached a traditional boat race in Sylhet and an Urs in Savar, with groups mobilising to have the events stopped.
Taken individually, the incidents have different circumstances and cannot all be attributed to the same actors or motive.
Together, however, they are feeding a growing fear among artists, cultural activists and academics: Bangladesh’s cultural space may be shrinking as organizers increasingly confront administrative uncertainty, ideological objections, mob pressure and the threat of violence.
That fear is particularly acute because at least 20 concerts or major live-music programs have been cancelled, postponed or forcibly stopped since August 2024 -- although some were disrupted for clearly unrelated reasons such as floods, weather or genuine crowd-safety concerns.
The latest disputes suggest the pressure is no longer confined to live music.
In Savar, protests have been lodged with the local administration and police demanding cancellation of an Urs scheduled for August 26-27.
In Beanibazar, Sylhet, a group operating under the banner of “Tawhidi Janata” has campaigned against an August 28 traditional boat race on the Sunai River and held a meeting at a local mosque demanding that it be stopped.
Bangladesh Udichi Shilpi Gosthi General Secretary Amit Ranjan Dey said concerts, films and traditional festivities were integral parts of Bangladesh’s diverse cultural identity.
“Such acts hinder the development of our culture,” he said, calling repeated attempts to stop cultural programs “shameful” and urging the government to act against groups obstructing them.
Dhaka University sociologist Tawohidul Haque said the consequences could extend beyond the programs already disrupted.
“We are observing with great concern that concerts are being closed and traditional events are being prevented in various places,” he said, warning that the incidents were creating fear and anxiety.
His greater concern is what happens next: repeated obstruction could eventually persuade people not to organize or attend cultural activities at all.
“Due to repeated obstacles, people will refrain from these things out of fear, resulting in the fear of the cultural sphere shrinking,” he said.
Independent MP Rumeen Farhana has also raised the issue in the National Parliament, accusing forces seeking to take Bangladesh “towards darkness” and portray it as a fundamentalist state of being behind such activities.
Concern has been reinforced by attacks on religious and folk-cultural sites.
Police previously reported 44 attacks on 40 shrines since August 2024, including vandalism and looting, with 23 people arrested in related criminal cases.
Following an attack on the Shah Ali shrine in Mirpur, Transparency International Bangladesh said such violence should not be treated as isolated, describing it as part of continuing attacks on folk traditions, pluralism and Bangladesh’s religious and cultural diversity.
Police Headquarters says it is monitoring groups attempting to obstruct cultural events.
AIG (Media and PR) AHM Shahadat Hossain said intelligence surveillance had been increased and local authorities had been instructed to remain alert over developments in Sylhet and Savar.
“No one will get away with committing a crime, and anyone who tries to create chaos will be dealt with severely,” he said.
Significantly, opposition to indiscriminate obstruction has also come from Islamic scholars.
Tanzimul Ummah Foundation Vice Chairman Meem Atiqullah said not every cultural or social ritual contradicted Islam and warned against preventing programs without properly understanding their nature.
“Islam does not teach anyone extremism,” he said, adding that Islam did not support excess or intolerance.
The emerging concern, therefore, is no longer simply whether another concert will be cancelled.
It is whether repeated pressure, threats and violence, and authorities’ willingness or inability to resist them, will gradually establish an informal veto over Bangladesh’s public cultural life.
For organizers, artists and audiences, that uncertainty itself risks becoming a restriction: a cultural program does not have to be formally banned if fear of the reaction is enough to stop it from being organized.
